title: Guitar versus banjo and the sound of Preservation Hall guitarists
summary: Allen and Russell on Sales's guitar, Bud Scott and Ory's band using guitar, and the dynamics of old bands.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Sales is loud. I was really surprised that I lied to you.
Ordinarily, Sales isn't real loud, like, say, as loud as Gayno, or...
Yeah, I mean, he was playing with Milford Dahlio, who's not a soft drummer.
I would never think of him, but... It was an electric, but Gale has an electric guitar, too. He has used it.
No, I think he got rid of his electric.
Years ago, yeah, but I think he got rid of all that stuff. He's gone back to acoustic in his product.
And I thought that was very interesting to hear, you know, cutting through the way he did, and you can hear the fullness of his sound on guitar.

Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of variety and dynamics, you might say. But that was part of the old New Orleans tradition, and Jelly talks about it, but Jelly also talks about they would be probably New Orleans bands, too. He was objecting to, being loud. Most of the bands today are that way, but not all of them. Even today, the bands today, when they play closer walk, they play some real soft muted trumpet solos and other things very soft sometimes. And a few of the spiritual numbers and other things will soften way down.
